content.content:
1	# wal-store
2	
3	Key value store that appends every mutation to a write-ahead log first, so a process killed between writes and checkpoints recovers exactly the committed state.
4	
5	## Requirements
6	
7	Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only.
8	
9	## Install
10	
11	    python3 -m pip install -e .
12	
13	## Run
14	
15	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store recover
16	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store put <key> --value-file <path>
17	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store get <key>
18	
19	## Public interface
20	
21	`wal_store.Store(path)` opens the store directory. The directory must
22	exist; opening a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` (the `put` command
23	line subcommand creates it).
24	- `put(key, value) -> None` records a mutation.
25	- `get(key) -> bytes | None` reads the value at the last committed snapshot.
26	- `delete(key) -> None` records a removal.
27	- `delete_range(start=None, end=None) -> None` records a batch removal of
28	  every committed key in a half-open byte range (`delete(start, end)` is
29	  the same call).
30	- `commit() -> int` advances the durable sequence number. Every call writes
31	  a commit marker and advances the sequence by exactly one, including a
32	  commit with no pending changes; the first commit after a compaction is the
33	  pre-compaction sequence plus one.
34	- `recover() -> dict` replays the log and reports what it applied.
35	- `compact() -> dict` rewrites committed history into one tight log and
36	  reclaims the old space, without changing the committed state or the
37	  durable sequence.
38	- `scan(start=None, end=None) -> ScanCursor` opens an ordered read-only
39	  cursor over the committed snapshot pinned at that moment.
40	- `ScanCursor.token() -> bytes` (alias `mark()`) serialises the cursor's
41	  current position into a resumable scan token; `scan(token=tok)`
42	  (alias `scan(resume=tok)`) continues that scan from the token.
43	- `stats() -> dict` reports sequence, entries and bytes.
44	
45	## Scanning
46	
47	`scan()` works on both open forms and never touches the write path. The
48	returned cursor is an iterator of `(key, value)` pairs in bytewise key
49	order — keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes and values come back as the
50	exact stored bytes, with no encoding conversion — covering `start`
51	inclusive through `end` exclusive; a `None` endpoint leaves that side
52	unbounded, so `scan()` walks everything. Keys that only ever appeared in
53	delete records never show up, a key overwritten any number of times yields
54	only its last committed value, and empty values scan like any other. A
55	writer's uncommitted changes are not part of the snapshot — they are
56	invisible to `scan()` and to `get()` alike, both of which read the last
57	committed snapshot; a read-only store scans the snapshot it pinned at open.
58	
59	The snapshot is materialised once when the cursor opens, so later commits,
60	compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space never
61	change what the cursor yields, and the same snapshot scans to the identical
62	sequence before and after compaction. Scanning never replays the log,
63	takes no lock and keeps no history in memory, so its cost is independent
64	of the log's length. A `start` that sorts after `end` raises `ValueError`,
65	as does reading from a cursor after `close()` (the cursor is also a
66	context manager).
67	
68	## Resumable scans
69	
70	A scan can be paused and later continued from exactly where it stopped, in
71	the same process or after reopening the store (writer or read-only). At any
72	point a cursor can serialise its current position into an opaque `bytes`
73	token:
74	
75	- `ScanCursor.token()` returns the token; `mark()` is an alias.
76	- `Store.scan(token=tok)` opens a new cursor that continues the identical
77	  range from the identical position over the identical snapshot;
78	  `scan(resume=tok)` is an alias. The token already carries its range, so
79	  passing `start`/`end` together with a token raises `ValueError`.
80	
81	Splitting one scan at a token and concatenating the pieces yields exactly
82	the pairs a single uninterrupted scan would have yielded, byte for byte:
83	the resumed stream is the tail of the original scan.
84	
85	The token names the snapshot it pins — the durable sequence number and a
86	content identity over the snapshot's canonical image — together with the
87	scan range and the next position. It stays valid across later commits,
88	compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space. When a
89	writer mints a token it durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an
90	immutable, content-addressed `wal.s<seq>.<id>` sidecar (an atomic write,
91	never edited in place), so the token keeps resolving after the underlying
92	log bytes are compacted away; snapshots that were never published can also
93	be reconstructed from the committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A
94	read-only store never publishes a snapshot copy when minting a token;
95	such a token still resolves because the writer has published (or can
96	reconstruct) that snapshot. The reader's only on-disk artifact is the
97	short-lived lease registered when its store or cursor opened, which keeps
98	that snapshot in use across processes for as long as the resumed scan is
99	alive.
100	
101	Deleted keys never come back. A token pins one exact committed snapshot:
102	resuming it reads precisely that snapshot, whether or not the same keys were
103	later deleted, and a range tombstone that compaction has since reclaimed
104	neither removes nor revives anything on the resumed path. A fresh scan of a
105	snapshot after the delete never shows the key.
106	
107	A token is opaque and strictly validated. Anything forged, truncated,
108	corrupted (checksum mismatch), carrying an out-of-range position, naming a
109	reversed range, or referring to a snapshot this store does not hold (a
110	foreign store, or a snapshot whose every copy has been reclaimed) raises
111	`ValueError`; nothing is guessed or repaired. A non-`bytes` token raises
112	`TypeError` — `bytearray` and `memoryview` are not accepted and are never
113	coerced. The token format is platform-independent: the same snapshot at
114	the same position always mints byte-identical tokens on Windows and Linux
115	(all integers are big-endian and no bytes are translated), so tokens can
116	be handed across platforms and processes.
117	
118	
119	## Historical snapshot lifecycle
120	
121	Minting a token publishes one immutable `wal.s<seq>.<id>` snapshot copy;
122	without lifecycle management those copies pile up forever, one per
123	minted snapshot. Reclamation fixes which copies survive and runs after
124	every commit and every compaction (and is finished at every writer open,
125	so a sweep killed mid-run simply completes on reopen):
126	
127	- **In use** — a copy is never reclaimed while any open cursor (including
128	  one merely iterating, with no token minted), any live read-only store or
129	  any resumed scan is serving that snapshot, in this process or in *any
130	  other process*. Cross-process users register a short-lived lease sidecar
131	  (`wal.lease.<pid>.<rand>`, the only kind of file a reader ever writes):
132	  it lists the snapshots that process has in use with a heartbeat, and the
133	  writer reads every lease before removing a copy (re-reading them
134	  immediately before each unlink, so a lease taken mid-sweep still
135	  protects its copy). An orderly close removes the lease; a process killed
136	  without closing stops heartbeating, and after the lease TTL its lease
137	  pins nothing and is swept. An in-use token keeps pointing at the same
138	  snapshot across commits, compactions and crash recovery; resuming it is
139	  byte-for-byte the tail of the original one-shot scan. Reclamation
140	  deletes only redundant copies — the reads and resumes in flight do not
141	  change by a byte, and a deleted key never comes back.
142	- **Always retained** — the current committed snapshot and the newest
143	  three published predecessor generations are never reclaimed.
144	- **Everything else** — copies outside the retention window with no user
145	  (no in-process pin and no fresh lease in any process) are deleted.
146	
147	A copy disappearing does not by itself invalidate a token: the token
148	keeps working for as long as that snapshot can still be rebuilt from the
149	committed log prefix or the checkpoint. Only once every copy is gone and
150	neither the surviving log prefix nor the checkpoint can rebuild the
151	snapshot does resuming an old token raise `ValueError`. Forged,
152	truncated, corrupted, out-of-range or cross-snapshot tokens raise
153	`ValueError` just as before; the store never guesses or repairs them.
154	
155	Reclamation is an idempotent convergence: independent file unlinks with
156	a directory sync at the end, so a kill at any point leaves a state the
157	next open converges to the identical file set. It cannot delete an
158	in-use copy (one named by an in-process pin or by any fresh lease),
159	cannot move the durable sequence or the committed state, and never
160	touches `wal.log`, `wal.ckp` or any record; it removes only dead
161	`wal.s<seq>.<id>` copies and, once expired, stale `wal.lease.*`
162	sidecars. Each lease sidecar is written only by its owner and is
163	atomically replaced (never edited in place), so registering, expiring
164	and reclaiming converge after a kill in any process to one in-use set
165	and one copy set. It adds no command-line subcommand: everything lives
166	in the same store directory behind the existing `scan`/token calls, and
167	the lease is the one kind of new file — a reader writes nothing else.
168	
169	
170	## Range deletes
171	
172	`delete_range(start=None, end=None)` removes every committed key a scan
173	of the same endpoints would return: keys compare by their raw UTF-8
174	bytes, the range is half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive) and a
175	`None` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so `delete_range()` clears
176	the whole store while `delete_range("a", "a")` removes nothing. The
177	shorthand `delete(start, end)` is the same call; `delete(key)` still
178	removes one key. Endpoint validation is shared with `scan`: non-string
179	endpoints raise `TypeError` and a `start` sorting after `end` raises
180	`ValueError`.
181	
182	Like every other mutation the tombstone is only staged in the session:
183	it is invisible to scans and read-only stores until `commit()`, and a
184	writer that is killed first reopens at the last committed state. Once
185	committed, the covered keys disappear from single-key reads and scans
186	alike, and a key that only ever appears in delete history can never come
187	back. Writing a key inside a previously deleted range simply stores the
188	new value — after commit it reads back as that last committed value,
189	with keys and values still handled as raw bytes.
190	
191	Recovery resolves a range tombstone by removing the covered keys; the
192	report counts the tombstone record under `applied`. Compaction reclaims
193	it together with the rest of the dead history: the compacted image
194	contains one live put per surviving key and no tombstones at all, so
195	reclaiming the record can never resurrect a deleted key, and a snapshot
196	scans to the identical bytes before and after compaction.
197	
198	## Read-only stores
199	
200	`wal_store.Store(path, read_only=True)` opens an isolated reader. Any
201	number of read-only processes may coexist with the single writer in the
202	same directory. A reader takes no lock and never touches the log, a
203	checkpoint or a snapshot copy; the only file it creates is its own
204	short-lived lease sidecar, registering the snapshots it has in use so a
205	writer in another process keeps them (best-effort — a read-only
206	directory simply has no lease, and the lease is removed again on close
207	or expires by heartbeat if the process is killed). It pins a snapshot at
208	open time and every `get` reads from that one complete committed
209	snapshot, so uncommitted mutations, a half-written commit, a torn record
210	or a half-finished shrink are never visible. Successive reads from the
211	same reader may advance across snapshots only by reopening; each read is
212	of one fully committed snapshot. Reads do not replay the log and do not
213	block the writer: killing or suspending a reader never affects the
214	writer's commits, recovery or stats (a killed reader leaves only a lease
215	that is ignored once stale and then swept). `put`, `delete`, `commit`
216	and `recover` are rejected on a read-only store; `stats` reports the
217	pinned snapshot and `get` is the normal way to read it. Readers serve
218	from the atomically replaced `wal.ckp` sidecar (and the committed log
219	prefix), so directories written by older versions open directly.
220	
221	`wal_store.inject_tear(source, destination, offset)` is a verification aid:
222	it writes a byte-for-byte copy of `source` cut at exactly `offset` bytes (a
223	replica of a process killed at that write position) to `destination` and
224	leaves the source untouched. Either argument may be a store directory, in
225	which case its `wal.log` is used. A negative or past-the-end offset raises
226	`IndexError`. It is never used by the normal write path.
227	
228	## Recovery
229	
230	`recover()` returns a report with three integer fields, in this key order:
231	
232	- `applied` — committed put/delete records replayed into the state,
233	- `discarded` — torn tail records dropped (at most one, the unfinished final
234	  write left by a process killed mid append; `0` on a clean log),
235	- `seq` — the durable sequence number after recovery.
236	
237	A record killed halfway through is not a mutation: it is discarded and the
238	recovered state is exactly the last committed state. An empty log recovers
239	to an empty state, which is a normal result. Recovery truncates the dirty
240	tail and the next commit uses `seq + 1`, no matter how often the store is
241	reopened.
242	
243	### Recovery may itself be killed
244	
245	Recovery is an idempotent, kill-safe convergence. Interrupting it at any
246	point — while the dirty tail is being dropped or the log is being rebuilt —
247	and reopening any number of times reaches exactly the state and the report
248	of one clean recovery, with exit code `0`; the durable sequence never
249	regresses and the next commit is always `seq + 1`.
250	
251	Two internal sidecar files in the store directory make this work; they are
252	not part of the public API and are maintained entirely below the write
253	path:
254	
255	- `wal.ckp` is an atomically replaced copy of the log prefix ending at the
256	  most recent commit marker. A log torn at *any* offset — even offset 0, or
257	  inside the committed prefix — is silently rebuilt from it, so a
258	  half-finished convergence can never be mistaken for a torn tail or for
259	  corruption.
260	- `wal.rec` is a small marker written after validation and before the
261	  repair, recording the clean prefix length and the discarded count. A
262	  repair interrupted mid-copy is simply repeated on reopen, and the marker
263	  keeps `discarded` stable across reopens and repeated recoveries until the
264	  next successful commit closes the epoch.
265	
266	Only the final record may be incomplete. Any incomplete record elsewhere,
267	a length out of bounds, unparseable content, or a duplicate/regressing
268	sequence is corruption: recovery raises `wal_store.CorruptLogError`
269	(a subclass of `ValueError`) and stops without applying or removing
270	anything.
271	
272	The command line `recover` prints the report as one compact JSON line with
273	the same key order and a trailing newline, e.g.
274	`{"applied":2,"discarded":0,"seq":1}`. Discarding a torn tail is not an
275	error and the exit code is `0`; corruption prints one explanatory line to
276	standard error and exits `3` without printing the JSON line.
277	
278	## Compaction
279	
280	`compact()` reclaims history without sacrificing any committed state. When
281	it finishes, the log contains exactly the live committed key/values: one
282	put frame per currently committed key, in sorted key order, followed by a
283	base commit marker that carries the pre-compaction sequence. Deleted keys
284	are gone for good — a deleted key can never reappear — and overwritten keys
285	keep only their final value. The durable sequence number is unchanged, so
286	the next `commit()` writes `seq + 1`; every commit advances, including an
287	empty one, and subsequent commits continue the strict sequence as if no

# wal-store

Key value store that appends every mutation to a write-ahead log first, so a process killed between writes and checkpoints recovers exactly the committed state.

## Requirements

Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only.

## Install

    python3 -m pip install -e .

## Run

    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store recover
    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store put <key> --value-file <path>
    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store get <key>

## Public interface

`wal_store.Store(path)` opens the store directory. The directory must
exist; opening a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` (the `put` command
line subcommand creates it).
- `put(key, value) -> None` records a mutation.
- `get(key) -> bytes | None` reads the value at the last committed snapshot.
- `delete(key) -> None` records a removal.
- `delete_range(start=None, end=None) -> None` records a batch removal of
  every committed key in a half-open byte range (`delete(start, end)` is
  the same call).
- `commit() -> int` advances the durable sequence number. Every call writes
  a commit marker and advances the sequence by exactly one, including a
  commit with no pending changes; the first commit after a compaction is the
  pre-compaction sequence plus one.
- `recover() -> dict` replays the log and reports what it applied.
- `compact() -> dict` rewrites committed history into one tight log and
  reclaims the old space, without changing the committed state or the
  durable sequence.
- `scan(start=None, end=None) -> ScanCursor` opens an ordered read-only
  cursor over the committed snapshot pinned at that moment.
- `ScanCursor.token() -> bytes` (alias `mark()`) serialises the cursor's
  current position into a resumable scan token; `scan(token=tok)`
  (alias `scan(resume=tok)`) continues that scan from the token.
- `stats() -> dict` reports sequence, entries and bytes.

## Scanning

`scan()` works on both open forms and never touches the write path. The
returned cursor is an iterator of `(key, value)` pairs in bytewise key
order — keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes and values come back as the
exact stored bytes, with no encoding conversion — covering `start`
inclusive through `end` exclusive; a `None` endpoint leaves that side
unbounded, so `scan()` walks everything. Keys that only ever appeared in
delete records never show up, a key overwritten any number of times yields
only its last committed value, and empty values scan like any other. A
writer's uncommitted changes are not part of the snapshot — they are
invisible to `scan()` and to `get()` alike, both of which read the last
committed snapshot; a read-only store scans the snapshot it pinned at open.

The snapshot is materialised once when the cursor opens, so later commits,
compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space never
change what the cursor yields, and the same snapshot scans to the identical
sequence before and after compaction. Scanning never replays the log,
takes no lock and keeps no history in memory, so its cost is independent
of the log's length. A `start` that sorts after `end` raises `ValueError`,
as does reading from a cursor after `close()` (the cursor is also a
context manager).

## Resumable scans

A scan can be paused and later continued from exactly where it stopped, in
the same process or after reopening the store (writer or read-only). At any
point a cursor can serialise its current position into an opaque `bytes`
token:

- `ScanCursor.token()` returns the token; `mark()` is an alias.
- `Store.scan(token=tok)` opens a new cursor that continues the identical
  range from the identical position over the identical snapshot;
  `scan(resume=tok)` is an alias. The token already carries its range, so
  passing `start`/`end` together with a token raises `ValueError`.

Splitting one scan at a token and concatenating the pieces yields exactly
the pairs a single uninterrupted scan would have yielded, byte for byte:
the resumed stream is the tail of the original scan.

The token names the snapshot it pins — the durable sequence number and a
content identity over the snapshot's canonical image — together with the
scan range and the next position. It stays valid across later commits,
compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space. When a
writer mints a token it durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an
immutable, content-addressed `wal.s<seq>.<id>` sidecar (an atomic write,
never edited in place), so the token keeps resolving after the underlying
log bytes are compacted away; snapshots that were never published can also
be reconstructed from the committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A
read-only store never publishes a snapshot copy when minting a token;
such a token still resolves because the writer has published (or can
reconstruct) that snapshot. The reader's only on-disk artifact is the
short-lived lease registered when its store or cursor opened, which keeps
that snapshot in use across processes for as long as the resumed scan is
alive.

Deleted keys never come back. A token pins one exact committed snapshot:
resuming it reads precisely that snapshot, whether or not the same keys were
later deleted, and a range tombstone that compaction has since reclaimed
neither removes nor revives anything on the resumed path. A fresh scan of a
snapshot after the delete never shows the key.

A token is opaque and strictly validated. Anything forged, truncated,
corrupted (checksum mismatch), carrying an out-of-range position, naming a
reversed range, or referring to a snapshot this store does not hold (a
foreign store, or a snapshot whose every copy has been reclaimed) raises
`ValueError`; nothing is guessed or repaired. A non-`bytes` token raises
`TypeError` — `bytearray` and `memoryview` are not accepted and are never
coerced. The token format is platform-independent: the same snapshot at
the same position always mints byte-identical tokens on Windows and Linux
(all integers are big-endian and no bytes are translated), so tokens can
be handed across platforms and processes.


## Historical snapshot lifecycle

Minting a token publishes one immutable `wal.s<seq>.<id>` snapshot copy;
without lifecycle management those copies pile up forever, one per
minted snapshot. Reclamation fixes which copies survive and runs after
every commit and every compaction (and is finished at every writer open,
so a sweep killed mid-run simply completes on reopen):

- **In use** — a copy is never reclaimed while any open cursor (including
  one merely iterating, with no token minted), any live read-only store or
  any resumed scan is serving that snapshot, in this process or in *any
  other process*. Cross-process users register a short-lived lease sidecar
  (`wal.lease.<pid>.<rand>`, the only kind of file a reader ever writes):
  it lists the snapshots that process has in use with a heartbeat, and the
  writer reads every lease before removing a copy (re-reading them
  immediately before each unlink, so a lease taken mid-sweep still
  protects its copy). An orderly close removes the lease; a process killed
  without closing stops heartbeating, and after the lease TTL its lease
  pins nothing and is swept. An in-use token keeps pointing at the same
  snapshot across commits, compactions and crash recovery; resuming it is
  byte-for-byte the tail of the original one-shot scan. Reclamation
  deletes only redundant copies — the reads and resumes in flight do not
  change by a byte, and a deleted key never comes back.
- **Always retained** — the current committed snapshot and the newest
  three published predecessor generations are never reclaimed.
- **Everything else** — copies outside the retention window with no user
  (no in-process pin and no fresh lease in any process) are deleted.

A copy disappearing does not by itself invalidate a token: the token
keeps working for as long as that snapshot can still be rebuilt from the
committed log prefix or the checkpoint. Only once every copy is gone and
neither the surviving log prefix nor the checkpoint can rebuild the
snapshot does resuming an old token raise `ValueError`. Forged,
truncated, corrupted, out-of-range or cross-snapshot tokens raise
`ValueError` just as before; the store never guesses or repairs them.

Reclamation is an idempotent convergence: independent file unlinks with
a directory sync at the end, so a kill at any point leaves a state the
next open converges to the identical file set. It cannot delete an
in-use copy (one named by an in-process pin or by any fresh lease),
cannot move the durable sequence or the committed state, and never
touches `wal.log`, `wal.ckp` or any record; it removes only dead
`wal.s<seq>.<id>` copies and, once expired, stale `wal.lease.*`
sidecars. Each lease sidecar is written only by its owner and is
atomically replaced (never edited in place), so registering, expiring
and reclaiming converge after a kill in any process to one in-use set
and one copy set. It adds no command-line subcommand: everything lives
in the same store directory behind the existing `scan`/token calls, and
the lease is the one kind of new file — a reader writes nothing else.


## Range deletes

`delete_range(start=None, end=None)` removes every committed key a scan
of the same endpoints would return: keys compare by their raw UTF-8
bytes, the range is half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive) and a
`None` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so `delete_range()` clears
the whole store while `delete_range("a", "a")` removes nothing. The
shorthand `delete(start, end)` is the same call; `delete(key)` still
removes one key. Endpoint validation is shared with `scan`: non-string
endpoints raise `TypeError` and a `start` sorting after `end` raises
`ValueError`.

Like every other mutation the tombstone is only staged in the session:
it is invisible to scans and read-only stores until `commit()`, and a
writer that is killed first reopens at the last committed state. Once
committed, the covered keys disappear from single-key reads and scans
alike, and a key that only ever appears in delete history can never come
back. Writing a key inside a previously deleted range simply stores the
new value — after commit it reads back as that last committed value,
with keys and values still handled as raw bytes.

Recovery resolves a range tombstone by removing the covered keys; the
report counts the tombstone record under `applied`. Compaction reclaims
it together with the rest of the dead history: the compacted image
contains one live put per surviving key and no tombstones at all, so
reclaiming the record can never resurrect a deleted key, and a snapshot
scans to the identical bytes before and after compaction.

## Read-only stores

`wal_store.Store(path, read_only=True)` opens an isolated reader. Any
number of read-only processes may coexist with the single writer in the
same directory. A reader takes no lock and never touches the log, a
checkpoint or a snapshot copy; the only file it creates is its own
short-lived lease sidecar, registering the snapshots it has in use so a
writer in another process keeps them (best-effort — a read-only
directory simply has no lease, and the lease is removed again on close
or expires by heartbeat if the process is killed). It pins a snapshot at
open time and every `get` reads from that one complete committed
snapshot, so uncommitted mutations, a half-written commit, a torn record
or a half-finished shrink are never visible. Successive reads from the
same reader may advance across snapshots only by reopening; each read is
of one fully committed snapshot. Reads do not replay the log and do not
block the writer: killing or suspending a reader never affects the
writer's commits, recovery or stats (a killed reader leaves only a lease
that is ignored once stale and then swept). `put`, `delete`, `commit`
and `recover` are rejected on a read-only store; `stats` reports the
pinned snapshot and `get` is the normal way to read it. Readers serve
from the atomically replaced `wal.ckp` sidecar (and the committed log
prefix), so directories written by older versions open directly.

`wal_store.inject_tear(source, destination, offset)` is a verification aid:
it writes a byte-for-byte copy of `source` cut at exactly `offset` bytes (a
replica of a process killed at that write position) to `destination` and
leaves the source untouched. Either argument may be a store directory, in
which case its `wal.log` is used. A negative or past-the-end offset raises
`IndexError`. It is never used by the normal write path.

## Recovery

`recover()` returns a report with three integer fields, in this key order:

- `applied` — committed put/delete records replayed into the state,
- `discarded` — torn tail records dropped (at most one, the unfinished final
  write left by a process killed mid append; `0` on a clean log),
- `seq` — the durable sequence number after recovery.

A record killed halfway through is not a mutation: it is discarded and the
recovered state is exactly the last committed state. An empty log recovers
to an empty state, which is a normal result. Recovery truncates the dirty
tail and the next commit uses `seq + 1`, no matter how often the store is
reopened.

### Recovery may itself be killed

Recovery is an idempotent, kill-safe convergence. Interrupting it at any
point — while the dirty tail is being dropped or the log is being rebuilt —
and reopening any number of times reaches exactly the state and the report
of one clean recovery, with exit code `0`; the durable sequence never
regresses and the next commit is always `seq + 1`.

Two internal sidecar files in the store directory make this work; they are
not part of the public API and are maintained entirely below the write
path:

- `wal.ckp` is an atomically replaced copy of the log prefix ending at the
  most recent commit marker. A log torn at *any* offset — even offset 0, or
  inside the committed prefix — is silently rebuilt from it, so a
  half-finished convergence can never be mistaken for a torn tail or for
  corruption.
- `wal.rec` is a small marker written after validation and before the
  repair, recording the clean prefix length and the discarded count. A
  repair interrupted mid-copy is simply repeated on reopen, and the marker
  keeps `discarded` stable across reopens and repeated recoveries until the
  next successful commit closes the epoch.

Only the final record may be incomplete. Any incomplete record elsewhere,
a length out of bounds, unparseable content, or a duplicate/regressing
sequence is corruption: recovery raises `wal_store.CorruptLogError`
(a subclass of `ValueError`) and stops without applying or removing
anything.

The command line `recover` prints the report as one compact JSON line with
the same key order and a trailing newline, e.g.
`{"applied":2,"discarded":0,"seq":1}`. Discarding a torn tail is not an
error and the exit code is `0`; corruption prints one explanatory line to
standard error and exits `3` without printing the JSON line.

## Compaction

`compact()` reclaims history without sacrificing any committed state. When
it finishes, the log contains exactly the live committed key/values: one
put frame per currently committed key, in sorted key order, followed by a
base commit marker that carries the pre-compaction sequence. Deleted keys
are gone for good — a deleted key can never reappear — and overwritten keys
keep only their final value. The durable sequence number is unchanged, so
the next `commit()` writes `seq + 1`; every commit advances, including an
empty one, and subsequent commits continue the strict sequence as if no
rewrite had happened. The empty committed state
(including "everything was deleted") compacts to an empty log.

`compact()` returns the same three-field report shape as `recover()`:
`applied` is the number of live puts the new log contains, `discarded` is
always `0` and `seq` is the preserved sequence. Uncommitted session changes
make it raise `ValueError`; commit or discard them first.

Compaction is a kill-safe, idempotent convergence like recovery. The new
image is assembled in memory and durably staged as the `wal.cmp` sidecar
(an atomically replaced complete file, never an in-place edit), then
published in two atomic steps — `wal.ckp` first and `wal.log` second —
before the staging file is removed. A process killed at any point, any
number of times, leaves a store that finishes the identical publish on the
next open: the recovered state is exactly the last committed state, the
sequence never regresses and the resulting log/sidecar bytes are
byte-identical to one uninterrupted compaction. Repeating compaction on an
already compact store produces the same bytes.

Live read-only stores are unaffected: they keep serving the complete
snapshot they pinned before, during and after compaction (it lands on the
other half of the same log-versus-checkpoint pair readers already choose
between), while fresh readers open the compacted snapshot. No reader ever
sees a mix of old and new bytes, a half-written file, or content whose
space was reclaimed; killing a reader does not disturb compaction and
killing the compactor does not disturb a reader. Compaction introduces no
new limits beyond the existing single-writer rule, and directories written
by older versions compact directly with no conversion step.

## Tests

    python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

## Limits

One writer at a time; no cross-process locking.
Values are bytes; encoding is the caller concern.
No replication; compaction is a writer-initiated rewrite, not background
garbage collection.

152	it as ``wal.ckp`` first and as ``wal.log`` second. Every intermediate state
153	is therefore either the pair of old files or the pair of complete new
154	images, which is precisely the two-image world the reader already chooses
155	between: a kill anywhere leaves a state reopening converges by simply
156	repeating the finish, and interrupting compaction any number of times
157	produces the same bytes as one clean run. Live readers keep serving their
158	pinned old snapshots (the inode survives on Unix; on Windows readers hold
159	no writer-side fd) and new readers land on the new snapshot, never a mix,
160	a half-written file or a byte that was already reclaimed.
161	
162	The durable commit boundary is the highest of the validated log boundary,
163	the checkpoint boundary and the marker boundary, so it can never move
164	backwards. Every repair step is either idempotent or an atomic rename; a
165	kill between any two steps leaves a state the next open converges from to
166	the identical result.
167	
168	Log frame layout (all integers big-endian)::
169	
170	    +---------+----------------+------------+----------------------+---------+
171	    | b"WAL2" | payload_length | header_crc | payload              | crc32   |
172	    | 4 bytes | 8 bytes        | 4 bytes    | metadata\\n<value>    | 4 bytes |
173	    +---------+----------------+------------+----------------------+---------+
174	
175	``header_crc`` is the crc32 of the magic and length bytes. It makes a
176	partial header that borrows bytes from a following frame fail validation,
177	so an incomplete record in the middle of the log reads as corruption while
178	a genuinely short final header reads as a torn tail.
179	
180	Metadata is a compact JSON object: ``{"t":"p","k":key}`` for puts,
181	``{"t":"d","k":key}`` for deletes, ``{"t":"r","s":start,"e":end}`` for
182	range tombstones (``null`` marks an unbounded side), ``{"t":"c","s":seq}``
183	for ordinary commits and ``{"t":"b","s":seq}`` for the base commit that
184	closes a compacted log. The two carry the sequence identically; a base
185	marker is additionally required to be the first commit marker in its file.
186	The raw value bytes follow the first newline, so values need no encoding.
187	
188	A range tombstone covers every committed key whose raw UTF-8 bytes sort at
189	or after its start and strictly before its end (half-open). It is resolved
190	when the log is replayed -- matching keys are popped then -- and, like an
191	ordinary delete frame, carries no state of its own. Compaction therefore
192	reclaims it together with every other dead record: the live puts the
193	compact image contains already exclude each deleted key, so dropping the
194	tombstone can never make one reappear.
195	"""

215	class CorruptLogError(ValueError):
216	    """The write-ahead log is corrupt, not merely missing a torn tail.
217	
218	    A single incomplete final record is a normal crash remnant and is
219	    discarded during recovery. Anything else that fails framing, checksum,
220	    metadata or commit-sequence validation is corruption; recovery stops
221	    without applying or removing anything.
222	    """

225	class ScanCursor:
226	    """Ordered read-only cursor over one pinned committed snapshot.
227	
228	    Created by :meth:`Store.scan`. Iterating yields ``(key, value)`` pairs
229	    in bytewise key order -- keys ordered by their raw UTF-8 bytes, values
230	    returned as the exact stored bytes -- covering the range given at open:
231	    the start key inclusive, the end key exclusive, either side unbounded
232	    when its endpoint was ``None``.
233	
234	    The snapshot is fully materialised when the cursor opens, so later
235	    commits, compaction, crash recovery or reclamation of the old log space
236	    never change what the cursor yields, and closing the store it came from
237	    does not disturb it. The cursor is an iterator; it is also a context
238	    manager, and ``close()`` releases the snapshot early. Reading from a
239	    closed cursor raises ``ValueError``.
240	
241	    :meth:`token` serialises the current position into an opaque ``bytes``
242	    token naming the pinned snapshot, the scan range and the next position.
243	    ``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in this process or in a freshly opened
244	    store -- continues the identical scan from that position.
245	    """
246	
247	    def __init__(self, items, lo_idx=0, hi_idx=None, pos=None, seq=0,
248	                 lo=None, hi=None, publisher=None, sid=None, leases=None):
249	        # ``items`` is the materialised snapshot: (key, value) pairs already
250	        # sorted by the keys' raw UTF-8 bytes. The visible window is
251	        # [lo_idx, hi_idx) and the next position starts at ``pos``.
252	        self._items = items
253	        self._lo_idx = lo_idx
254	        self._hi_idx = len(items) if hi_idx is None else hi_idx
255	        self._pos = lo_idx if pos is None else pos
256	        self._seq = seq
257	        self._lo = lo
258	        self._hi = hi
259	        # Writer-only callback durably publishing the pinned snapshot so a
260	        # minted token survives compaction and reclamation; ``None`` on
261	        # read-only stores, which never create or modify any file.
262	        self._publisher = publisher
263	        self._sid = sid
264	        # An open cursor counts as a user of its snapshot for the
265	        # reclamation rules: its box keeps the snapshot's pin alive in the
266	        # process-wide pin set until ``close()`` (or destruction), so
267	        # reclamation never removes the copy an open cursor is over. The
268	        # content identity is derived lazily on the first token mint.
269	        self._box = _register_snapshot(seq, items, sid)
270	        # On a read-only store the cursor additionally holds a cross-process
271	        # lease for its pinned snapshot (``leases`` is the store's lease
272	        # registry), so a writer in another process treats it as in use. The
273	        # identity is already known there. A writer cursor passes no lease
274	        # registry: its pin is visible to the reclaimer directly in-process.
275	        self._leases = leases
276	        self._lease_held = False
277	        self._lease_finalizer = None
278	        # Only a snapshot that actually has a published copy (seq >= 1) can
279	        # need cross-process protection.
280	        if leases is not None and sid is not None and seq >= 1:
281	            leases.acquire(seq, sid)
282	            self._lease_held = True
283	            # A cursor dropped without close() must release its lease the way
284	            # its weak in-process pin releases on GC.
285	            self._lease_finalizer = weakref.finalize(
286	                self, _release_lease, leases, seq, sid)
287	        self._closed = False
288	
289	    def __iter__(self) -> "ScanCursor":
290	        return self
291	
292	    def __next__(self):
293	        if self._closed:
294	            raise ValueError("scan cursor is closed")
295	        if self._pos >= self._hi_idx:
296	            raise StopIteration
297	        item = self._items[self._pos]
298	        self._pos += 1
299	        return item
300	
301	    def token(self) -> bytes:
302	        """Serialise the current position into an opaque scan token.
303	
304	        The returned ``bytes`` name the pinned snapshot (its durable
305	        sequence number and content identity), the scan range and the next
306	        position. Feeding the token to ``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in this
307	        process or in a freshly opened store, writer or read-only -- opens
308	        a cursor that continues the same range from the same position over
309	        the same pinned snapshot, byte-identical to the tail of this scan.
310	
311	        Token bytes are platform-independent and deterministic: the same
312	        snapshot at the same position always mints the same token. On a
313	        writer store minting also publishes the pinned snapshot as an
314	        immutable sidecar so the token survives compaction and reclamation
315	        of the old log space; a read-only store never publishes a snapshot
316	        copy when minting (it only holds the cross-process lease registered
317	        when the cursor opened).
318	        """
319	        if self._closed:
320	            raise ValueError("scan cursor is closed")
321	        if self._sid is None:
322	            self._sid = _snapshot_id(self._items)
323	            # Share the derived identity with the pin box so the in-use
324	            # check at reclamation never hashes this snapshot again.
325	            self._box._sid = self._sid
326	        if self._publisher is not None:
327	            self._publisher(self._seq, self._sid, self._items)
328	        return _encode_token(self._seq, self._sid, self._lo, self._hi,
329	                             self._pos)
330	
331	    def mark(self) -> bytes:
332	        """Alias for :meth:`token`."""
333	        return self.token()
334	
335	    @property
336	    def closed(self) -> bool:
337	        return self._closed
338	
339	    def close(self) -> None:
340	        if self._closed:
341	            return
342	        _unpin_snapshot(self._box)
343	        if self._lease_held:
344	            # Detach the GC finalizer: this explicit release is the one.
345	            if self._lease_finalizer is not None:
346	                self._lease_finalizer.detach()
347	            self._leases.release(self._seq, self._sid)
348	            self._lease_held = False
349	        self._items = []
350	        self._box = None
351	        self._closed = True
352	
353	    def __enter__(self) -> "ScanCursor":
354	        return self
355	
356	    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) -> None:
357	        self.close()

360	LOG_NAME = "wal.log"
361	_CHECKPOINT_NAME = "wal.ckp"
362	_MARKER_NAME = "wal.rec"
363	_COMPACT_NAME = "wal.cmp"
364	
365	_MAGIC = b"WAL2"
366	_PREFIX = 12  # 4 bytes magic + 8 bytes payload length
367	_HEADER = 16   # prefix + 4 bytes crc32 of the prefix
368	_TRAILER = 4   # crc32 of the payload
369	_MAX_PAYLOAD = 1 << 40
370	
371	_OP_PUT = "p"
372	_OP_DELETE = "d"
373	_OP_RANGE = "r"
374	_OP_COMMIT = "c"
375	_OP_BASE = "b"
376	_COMMIT_OPS = (_OP_COMMIT, _OP_BASE)
377	_OP_SNAP = "s"  # header frame of a pinned-snapshot sidecar
378	
379	# Pinned-snapshot sidecars (``wal.s<seq>.<id>``) and scan tokens. A token
380	# is an opaque, platform-independent byte string: magic, the snapshot's
381	# durable sequence, its 32-byte content identity, the optional range
382	# endpoints, the next position and a checksum -- all integers big-endian,
383	# so the same snapshot and position mint byte-identical tokens everywhere.
384	_TOKEN_MAGIC = b"WST1"
385	_SNAPSHOT_PREFIX = "wal.s"
386	_EMPTY_SNAPSHOT_ID = hashlib.sha256(b"").digest()
387	# Besides the snapshot the store is currently committed at, the newest this
388	# many published snapshot copies are always retained; older copies are
389	# reclaimed once nothing is using them.
390	_SNAPSHOT_RETENTION = 3
391	
392	# Cross-process in-use registration. The in-process pin set only names users
393	# in the opening process, so a snapshot pinned by a cursor or a read-only
394	# store in *another* process would look free to this writer's reclamation.
395	# Each lease-holding process therefore owns one short-lived sidecar of the
396	# single ``wal.lease.*`` kind: it lists the snapshots that process has in use
397	# together with a heartbeat timestamp, and is atomically rewritten in place.
398	# The writer reads every lease sidecar before removing a copy and treats
399	# every fresh one as an in-use pin. An orderly close removes the file; a
400	# process killed without closing stops heartbeating, so once its timestamp
401	# is older than the TTL it pins nothing and its stale sidecar is swept.
402	_LEASE_PREFIX = "wal.lease."
403	_LEASE_REC_PREFIX = "wal.l"
404	_LEASE_HEARTBEAT = 0.5
405	_LEASE_TTL = 5.0
406	_LEASE_SID_HEX = 64
407	_LEASE_SEQ_MAX = 20
408	_LEASE_TS_LEN = 16
409	# "wal.l<seq20>.<sid64>.<ts16>\n" -- one fixed-width record per pinned
410	# snapshot. A sidecar is always one or more whole records because it is
411	# published only by a temp-file/rename, so a reader can never see a torn one.
412	_LEASE_REC_LEN = (len(_LEASE_REC_PREFIX) + _LEASE_SEQ_MAX + 1
413	                  + _LEASE_SID_HEX + 1 + _LEASE_TS_LEN + 1)

416	def _snapshot_image(items) -> bytes:
417	    """Canonical byte image of a committed snapshot: one put frame per key.
418	
419	    ``items`` must already be sorted by the keys' raw UTF-8 bytes. The
420	    image uses the same deterministic framing as the log, so it is
421	    identical on every platform for the same snapshot.
422	    """
423	    return b"".join(_encode_frame(_OP_PUT, value, key=key)
424	                    for key, value in items)
425	
426	
427	def _snapshot_id(items) -> bytes:
428	    """Content identity of a committed snapshot (32 raw bytes)."""
429	    return hashlib.sha256(_snapshot_image(items)).digest()

432	def _encode_token(seq: int, sid: bytes, lo: bytes | None,
433	                  hi: bytes | None, pos: int) -> bytes:
434	    """Serialise a scan position; the exact inverse of :func:`_decode_token`."""
435	    flags = (1 if lo is not None else 0) | (2 if hi is not None else 0)
436	    parts = [_TOKEN_MAGIC, seq.to_bytes(8, "big"), sid, bytes((flags,))]
437	    for bound in (lo, hi):
438	        raw = bound if bound is not None else b""
439	        parts.append(len(raw).to_bytes(4, "big"))
440	        parts.append(raw)
441	    parts.append(pos.to_bytes(8, "big"))
442	    body = b"".join(parts)
443	    return body + zlib.crc32(body).to_bytes(4, "big")
444

446	def _decode_token(tok: bytes):
447	    """Parse a scan token into ``(seq, sid, lo, hi, pos)``.
448	
449	    Every malformation -- wrong magic, truncation, trailing garbage, a
450	    checksum mismatch, unknown flags, a hidden endpoint or a reversed
451	    range -- raises ``ValueError``; nothing is guessed or repaired.
452	    """
453	    if len(tok) < 4 + 8 + 32 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 8 + 4:
454	        raise ValueError("not a scan token")
455	    if tok[:4] != _TOKEN_MAGIC:
456	        raise ValueError("not a scan token")
457	    if int.from_bytes(tok[-4:], "big") != zlib.crc32(tok[:-4]):
458	        raise ValueError("scan token checksum mismatch")
459	    off = 4
460	    seq = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 8], "big")
461	    off += 8
462	    sid = tok[off:off + 32]
463	    off += 32
464	    flags = tok[off]
465	    off += 1
466	    if flags & ~0x03:
467	        raise ValueError("scan token carries unknown flags")
468	    bounds = []
469	    for present in (flags & 1, flags & 2):
470	        if off + 4 > len(tok) - 4:
471	            raise ValueError("scan token is truncated")
472	        size = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 4], "big")
473	        off += 4
474	        if off + size > len(tok) - 4:
475	            raise ValueError("scan token is truncated")
476	        if not present and size != 0:
477	            raise ValueError("scan token carries a hidden endpoint")
478	        bounds.append(tok[off:off + size] if present else None)
479	        off += size
480	    if off + 8 != len(tok) - 4:
481	        raise ValueError("scan token length mismatch")
482	    pos = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 8], "big")
483	    lo, hi = bounds
484	    if lo is not None and hi is not None and lo > hi:
485	        raise ValueError("scan token range is reversed")
486	    return seq, sid, lo, hi, pos

489	class _SnapshotBox:
490	    """Strong box around one user's materialised, pinned snapshot.
491	
492	    A box is the unit the reclamation logic counts as a user: every open
493	    cursor and every read-only store holds its own box for the snapshot it
494	    serves. Boxes live in a process-wide :class:`weakref.WeakSet`, so a
495	    cursor or reader that is garbage collected without an explicit
496	    ``close()`` releases its pin automatically -- the in-use table can
497	    neither leak nor outlive the snapshots it protects. The content
498	    identity is hashed lazily, so merely opening a scan that never mints a
499	    token pays no hashing cost.
500	    """
501	
502	    __slots__ = ("seq", "items", "_sid", "__weakref__")
503	
504	    def __init__(self, seq, items, sid=None):
505	        self.seq = seq
506	        self.items = items
507	        self._sid = sid
508	
509	    def sid(self) -> bytes:
510	        if self._sid is None:
511	            self._sid = _snapshot_id(self.items)
512	        return self._sid
513	
514	
515	# Process-wide set of snapshots currently in use. Every open cursor and
516	# every live read-only store keeps a box here for its pinned snapshot; the
517	# writer's reclamation never removes the published copy of any snapshot
518	# named in this set. The set is weak, so users closed normally (or simply
519	# dropped) release their pin with no bookkeeping. The boxes also keep the
520	# materialised bytes alive in memory, so a token minted in this process
521	# resolves without touching disk even across stores.
522	_PINS: "weakref.WeakSet" = weakref.WeakSet()
523	
524	
525	def _register_snapshot(seq: int, items, sid=None) -> _SnapshotBox:
526	    """Register one user (a cursor or a reader) pinning a snapshot."""
527	    box = _SnapshotBox(seq, items, sid)
528	    _PINS.add(box)
529	    return box
530	
531	
532	def _unpin_snapshot(box: _SnapshotBox) -> None:
533	    """Release the pin held by a closing cursor or reader."""
534	    _PINS.discard(box)
535	
536	
537	def _release_lease(leases, seq: int, sid: bytes) -> None:
538	    """Release a GC'd cursor's cross-process lease; never raises.
539	
540	    A cursor dropped without ``close()`` releases its in-process pin through
541	    the weak pin set; this gives the same treatment to its cross-process
542	    lease so a forgotten cursor cannot pin a copy forever.
543	    """
544	    try:
545	        leases.release(seq, sid)
546	    except Exception:
547	        # Finalizers must never raise into the garbage collector.
548	        pass
549	
550	
551	def _live_snapshot_keys() -> set:
552	    """The ``(seq, sid)`` pairs with at least one user in this process."""
553	    return {(box.seq, box.sid()) for box in _PINS}
554	
555	
556	def _pinned_snapshot(seq: int, sid: bytes):
557	    """Materialised items for a live in-process pin, or ``None``.
558	
559	    The identity is compared only for boxes already on the token's
560	    sequence, so a resolution against an unpinned sequence hashes nothing.
561	    """
562	    for box in _PINS:
563	        if box.seq == seq and box.sid() == sid:
564	            return box.items
565	    return None

568	class _LeaseManager:
569	    """Cross-process registry of snapshots currently in use.
570	
571	    A process that opens a read-only store or holds a cursor over some
572	    snapshot owns exactly one lease sidecar --
573	    ``wal.lease.<pid>.<rand>``, all of the single ``wal.lease.*`` kind --
574	    listing every snapshot that process has in use, one fixed-width
575	    ``wal.l<seq>.<sid>.<heartbeat>\\n`` record each. The file is rewritten
576	    atomically (temp file, rename; no fsync, because a lease need not
577	    survive a crash) on every change and every heartbeat, so another
578	    process never observes a half-written record: what it reads is one
579	    complete lease image or the previous one.
580	
581	    Because each process writes only its own file, registering, refreshing
582	    and removing a lease never races another process's lease. An orderly
583	    ``close()`` deletes the sidecar; a process killed without closing simply
584	    stops heartbeating, and the writer then ignores every record whose
585	    timestamp is older than the TTL and sweeps the stale file. The writer
586	    reads *all* lease sidecars before reclaiming a copy, so a snapshot a
587	    cursor or a read-only store in any process is serving is never removed.
588	
589	    A lease is a protection, never a requirement: writes are best-effort, so
590	    a read-only directory simply has no sidecar and reading is unaffected,
591	    while the in-process pins still apply.
592	    """
593	
594	    def __init__(self, directory: str):
595	        self._dir = directory
596	        # A unique name per process instance. The random suffix keeps two
597	        # incarnations of one pid (pid reuse, or processes sharing a copied
598	        # directory) from ever touching one sidecar.
599	        self._name = f"{_LEASE_PREFIX}{os.getpid()}.{uuid.uuid4().hex}"
600	        self._path = os.path.join(directory, self._name)
601	        # Snapshot keys this process currently leases, reference counted: a
602	        # read-only store and each of its cursors pin independently, so one
603	        # key stays registered until every holder has released it.
604	        self._counts: dict[tuple[int, bytes], int] = {}
605	        self._lock = threading.Lock()
606	        self._stop = threading.Event()
607	        self._thread = None
608	        self._disabled = False
609	
610	    def __del__(self) -> None:
611	        # Defensive backstop: if a manager is collected while it still lists
612	        # keys (its holders' explicit releases and finalizers normally clear
613	        # these first), drop the sidecar. The daemon heartbeat thread, while
614	        # alive, holds a reference to this manager, so by here it has exited.
615	        try:
616	            if getattr(self, "_counts", None):
617	                self._remove_locked()
618	                self._stop.set()
619	        except Exception:
620	            pass
621	
622	    # -- record format -----------------------------------------------------
623	
624	    @staticmethod
625	    def _record(seq: int, sid: bytes, now: float) -> bytes:
626	        # Microseconds since the epoch as a fixed 16-digit integer: exactly
627	        # 16 digits for every realistic date (no variable-width decimal
628	        # point), so every record is one constant width on every platform.
629	        ts = str(int(now * 1_000_000)).rjust(_LEASE_TS_LEN, "0")[-_LEASE_TS_LEN:]
630	        return (f"{_LEASE_REC_PREFIX}{seq:0{_LEASE_SEQ_MAX}d}."
631	                f"{sid.hex()}.").encode("ascii") + ts.encode("ascii") + b"\n"
632	
633	    def _image(self, now: float) -> bytes:
634	        return b"".join(self._record(seq, sid, now)
635	                        for seq, sid in sorted(self._counts))
636	
637	    def _publish(self, now: float | None = None) -> None:
638	        """Atomically write this process's current lease image.
639	
640	        Temp file plus a rename, deliberately *without* fsync: a lease only
641	        has to be visible to a concurrently running writer, never to survive
642	        a crash -- a crashed owner's lease is treated as stale regardless,
643	        and a machine crash leaves no live owner at all. Skipping the fsync
644	        (and the directory sync) keeps a read-only open and each heartbeat
645	        cheap, while the rename still guarantees the writer reads either the
646	        previous complete image or the new one, never a torn file.
647	        """
648	        if self._disabled:
649	            return
650	        if now is None:
651	            now = time.time()
652	        tmp = self._path + ".tmp"
653	        try:
654	            with open(tmp, "wb") as f:
655	                f.write(self._image(now))
656	            os.replace(tmp, self._path)
657	        except OSError:
658	            # A read-only directory can never host a lease: stop trying so a
659	            # reader there stays free of repeated failing writes. Any other
660	            # OSError (e.g. a brief Windows rename collision with a concurrent
661	            # reader of the file) is transient -- leave the lease enabled and
662	            # let the next heartbeat republish it, so a live holder is never
663	            # mistaken for a dead one.
664	            if not os.access(self._dir, os.W_OK):
665	                self._disabled = True
666	            try:
667	                os.unlink(tmp)
668	            except OSError:
669	                pass
670	
671	    # -- lease lifecycle ---------------------------------------------------
672	
673	    def acquire(self, seq: int, sid: bytes) -> None:
674	        """Take one reference on the lease for ``(seq, sid)``.
675	
676	        Idempotent across the holders of one process (a read-only store and
677	        each of its cursors): the key is registered once on disk but stays
678	        until every holder has released it.
679	        """
680	        if sid is None or seq < 1:
681	            # The empty initial snapshot (seq 0) never has a published copy
682	            # and so never needs a lease.
683	            return
684	        key = (seq, sid)
685	        with self._lock:
686	            count = self._counts.get(key, 0) + 1
687	            self._counts[key] = count
688	            if count == 1:
689	                self._publish()
690	                self._start_locked()
691	
692	    def release(self, seq: int, sid: bytes) -> None:
693	        """Drop one holder's reference; remove the lease at zero. Best effort."""
694	        if sid is None or seq < 1:
695	            return
696	        key = (seq, sid)
697	        thread = None
698	        with self._lock:
699	            count = self._counts.get(key, 0)
700	            if count == 0:
701	                return
702	            if count > 1:
703	                self._counts[key] = count - 1
704	                self._publish()
705	                return
706	            del self._counts[key]
707	            if self._counts:
708	                self._publish()
709	            else:
710	                self._remove_locked()
711	                thread = self._thread
712	                self._stop.set()
713	                self._thread = None

782	        seq_field = body[:_LEASE_SEQ_MAX]
783	        dot1 = body[_LEASE_SEQ_MAX:_LEASE_SEQ_MAX + 1]
784	        sid_field = body[_LEASE_SEQ_MAX + 1:_LEASE_SEQ_MAX + 1 + _LEASE_SID_HEX]

991	def _iter_frames(f):
992	    """Scan an open binary log file from position 0.
993	
994	    For every intact frame yields
995	    ``("frame", meta, value, start, end)``. Scanning stops with either no
996	    terminal event (clean EOF), ``("torn", start)`` for a single incomplete
997	    final frame, or ``("invalid", start)`` for a frame that fails framing,
998	    header/payload checksum or metadata parsing. With the header checksum a
999	    partial header that borrows bytes from a following record cannot survive,
1000	    so a short read landing exactly at EOF is reliably the one unfinished
1001	    record a single writer was appending when it died; bytes left beyond such
1002	    a read instead make it corruption.
1003	    """
1004	    f.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
1005	    eof = f.tell()
1006	    f.seek(0)
1007	    while True:
1008	        start = f.tell()
1009	        header = f.read(_HEADER)
1010	        if not header:
1011	            return
1012	        if len(header) < _HEADER:
1013	            # Trailing bytes of a frame header are a torn tail only when
1014	            # nothing follows them; a gap anywhere else is corruption.
1015	            yield (("torn", start) if f.tell() == eof
1016	                   else ("invalid", start))
1017	            return
1018	        if header[:4] != _MAGIC:
1019	            yield "invalid", start
1020	            return
1021	        if int.from_bytes(header[_PREFIX:], "big") != zlib.crc32(
1022	                header[:_PREFIX]):
1023	            yield "invalid", start
1024	            return
1025	        length = int.from_bytes(header[4:_PREFIX], "big")
1026	        if length > _MAX_PAYLOAD:
1027	            yield "invalid", start
1028	            return
1029	        payload = f.read(length)
1030	        checksum = f.read(_TRAILER)
1031	        if len(payload) < length or len(checksum) < _TRAILER:
1032	            # Only the single final record may be incomplete.
1033	            yield (("torn", start) if f.tell() == eof
1034	                   else ("invalid", start))
1035	            return
1036	        if int.from_bytes(checksum, "big") != zlib.crc32(payload):
1037	            yield "invalid", start
1038	            return
1039	        newline = payload.find(b"\n")
1040	        if newline < 0:
1041	            yield "invalid", start
1042	            return
1043	        try:
1044	            meta = json.loads(payload[:newline])
1045	        except (ValueError, UnicodeDecodeError):
1046	            yield "invalid", start
1047	            return
1048	        if not isinstance(meta, dict) or not isinstance(meta.get("t"), str):
1049	            yield "invalid", start
1050	            return
1051	        yield "frame", meta, payload[newline + 1:], start, f.tell()

"""Write-ahead log key value store.

Every mutation is first appended to a framed log. A commit marker is the
only thing that advances the durable sequence number, and every
``commit()`` writes one -- including an empty commit with nothing pending,
which advances the sequence by exactly one like any other commit. When a
store is opened, any tail that was never committed (including a record
torn by a hard kill) is discarded, so recovery always yields exactly the
committed state. Single-key reads and scans of a writer both see only the
last committed snapshot; uncommitted session changes are invisible to
either.

Only the very last log record may be incomplete: a process killed while
appending leaves at most one torn record, which is dropped without being
applied. Any other framing failure -- a truncated record in the middle, a
length field out of bounds, unparseable content, or a duplicate/regressing
commit sequence -- is corruption, and recovery raises ``CorruptLogError``
without touching the store.

Recovery itself may be killed at any point, any number of times. Two small
sidecar files in the store directory, both maintained below the write path,
make the convergence protocol kill-safe and its report stable:

``wal.ckp``
    A byte-for-byte copy of the log prefix ending at the most recent commit
    marker, replaced atomically (temp file, fsync, rename, directory fsync)
    only after that commit frame is durable. A log torn at *any* offset --
    even offset 0, or inside the committed prefix -- is rebuilt from it, so
    the durable sequence number never regresses. It is also the published
    snapshot read-only processes pin (see below).

``wal.rec``
    A recovery marker written only after a log needing repair has passed
    full validation and only *before* the atomic rebuild starts. It records
    the clean prefix length and whether a torn record was discarded. Its
    presence makes a rebuild interrupted mid-copy converge on reopen (the
    rebuild is simply repeated) and keeps the reported ``discarded`` count
    stable across reopens and repeated recoveries. It is removed by the next
    successful commit.

Range scans (``Store.scan(start, end)``) open an ordered read-only cursor
over the complete committed snapshot pinned at the moment the cursor is
opened. The cursor yields ``(key, value)`` pairs in bytewise key order --
keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes, with no encoding conversion -- from
``start`` (inclusive) to ``end`` (exclusive); a ``None`` endpoint leaves
that side unbounded. Keys that only ever appear in delete records never
show up, a key overwritten many times yields only its last committed value,
and empty values scan like any other. The snapshot is materialised once
when the cursor opens, so commits, compaction or crash recovery during the
scan never change it, reclaiming the old log space cannot break it, and the
cost of a scan is independent of how long the log's history is. A reversed
range (``start`` after ``end``) and any read from a closed cursor raise
``ValueError``.

A cursor's position serialises into an opaque ``bytes`` token via
``ScanCursor.token()``. The token names the pinned snapshot -- its durable
sequence number and a content identity over the snapshot's canonical image
-- together with the scan range and the next position. Passing it back as
``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in the same process or in a freshly opened
store, writer or read-only -- continues the identical range from the
identical position over the identical snapshot, so the resumed stream is
byte-for-byte the tail of the original scan. Tokens stay valid across
later commits, compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log
space: a writer durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an immutable
``wal.s<seq>.<id>`` sidecar when a token is minted, and snapshots that
were never published still resolve from the committed log prefix or the
checkpoint. Deleted keys -- including keys covered by range tombstones
that compaction has since reclaimed -- never reappear: the resumed stream
is always exactly the pinned snapshot. A token that is forged, truncated,
corrupted, out of range or names a snapshot the store does not hold raises
``ValueError`` with no guessing or repair; only genuine ``bytes`` are
accepted (a ``bytearray`` or ``memoryview`` raises ``TypeError``), and the
token bytes are platform-independent and identical for the same snapshot
and position.

Published snapshot copies have a lifecycle of their own, so the store
directory does not grow one permanent copy per minted token. Reclamation
runs after every commit and every compaction and is finished at every
writer open. A copy survives while it is *in use* -- an open cursor, a
live read-only store, or a resumed scan in this process or *any other
process*, is serving that snapshot -- and the current committed snapshot
together with the newest three published predecessor generations are
always retained; every other copy is removed. The in-process pin set is
process-wide and weak, so a writer and the read-only stores (or cursors)
in the same process share one notion of "in use", and a cursor dropped
without ``close()`` releases its pin when it is garbage collected.

The in-process pin set cannot see users in other processes, so every
read-only store, cursor and resume session additionally registers a
short-lived *lease* -- the one kind of sidecar a reader is allowed to
write, named ``wal.lease.<pid>.<rand>`` -- listing the snapshots that
process has in use with a heartbeat. The writer reads all lease sidecars
before reclaiming a copy (re-reading them immediately before each unlink,
so a lease taken mid-sweep still protects its copy) and keeps every copy a
fresh lease names. An orderly close removes the sidecar; a process killed
without closing simply stops heartbeating, and after the lease TTL its
sidecar pins nothing and is swept. Each lease sidecar is atomically
rewritten (temp file, rename) and only its owner ever writes it, so
registering, expiring and reclaiming -- with a kill at any point, reopened
in any process -- converge to the same in-use set and the same copy set.
Lease writes are best-effort, so a genuinely read-only directory simply
has no lease.

Reclamation deletes only redundant copies, never the log, the checkpoint
or a record, and changes neither the durable sequence nor the committed
state; the sweep is a set of independent unlinks followed by a directory
sync, so a kill at any point and a reopen converges to the same file set.
Losing a copy does not invalidate its token while the snapshot can still
be rebuilt from the log prefix or the checkpoint; only once no copy
remains and neither durable source can rebuild it does an old token stop
resolving (``ValueError``).


Range deletes (``Store.delete_range(start, end)``, or ``delete(start,
end)``) use the very same endpoints and half-open bytewise convention as
scans: after the next commit, every key a scan of ``[start, end)`` would
have returned is gone -- from single-key reads and scans alike -- while a
``None`` endpoint leaves that side unbounded and a reversed range raises
``ValueError`` through the shared endpoint check. The tombstone is staged
like any other mutation: until committed it is invisible to scans and
readers and a crash discards it. A key written inside a previously
deleted range simply keeps its new value, and keys that only ever appear
in delete history never come back -- recovery resolves the tombstone by
removing the covered keys and compaction drops the record entirely, so no
deleted key can ever be resurrected.

Read-only processes (``Store(path, read_only=True)``) take no lock and never
touch the log, the checkpoint or any snapshot copy: the only file a reader
creates is its own short-lived lease sidecar (best-effort, and absent
altogether in a read-only directory). At open each one picks the highest
committed prefix available at that instant -- the validated ``wal.log``
prefix or ``wal.ckp`` -- scans it once into memory and serves every ``get``
from that index. Because the chosen image is complete and is only ever
replaced atomically (never edited in place), a refresh caught mid-rename, a
half-written commit, a torn record, or a log being rebuilt, shrunk or
compacted can never expose partial bytes: each read lands on one full
committed snapshot that was current at or after the open. A directory
written by an older version is opened the same way from its log and
checkpoint. Reads never replay the log afterwards, so their cost is
independent of history and they never block the writer; a reader that hangs
changes no data, and one that is killed merely leaves a lease that expires
by heartbeat and is swept, never affecting the committed state.

Compaction (``Store.compact()``) rewrites the committed history into one
tight image without losing a byte of committed state. The compacted log
holds exactly the live puts -- one per currently committed key, in sorted
key order -- followed by a *base commit* marker carrying the pre-compaction
sequence number. The durable sequence keeps that value, so the next commit
is ``seq + 1`` and every later commit continues the strict sequence; keys
that were deleted never come back. The image is assembled in memory and
staged as the atomically replaced ``wal.cmp`` sidecar; finishing installs
it as ``wal.ckp`` first and as ``wal.log`` second. Every intermediate state
is therefore either the pair of old files or the pair of complete new
images, which is precisely the two-image world the reader already chooses
between: a kill anywhere leaves a state reopening converges by simply
repeating the finish, and interrupting compaction any number of times
produces the same bytes as one clean run. Live readers keep serving their
pinned old snapshots (the inode survives on Unix; on Windows readers hold
no writer-side fd) and new readers land on the new snapshot, never a mix,
a half-written file or a byte that was already reclaimed.

The durable commit boundary is the highest of the validated log boundary,
the checkpoint boundary and the marker boundary, so it can never move
backwards. Every repair step is either idempotent or an atomic rename; a
kill between any two steps leaves a state the next open converges from to
the identical result.

Log frame layout (all integers big-endian)::

    +---------+----------------+------------+----------------------+---------+
    | b"WAL2" | payload_length | header_crc | payload              | crc32   |
    | 4 bytes | 8 bytes        | 4 bytes    | metadata\\n<value>    | 4 bytes |
    +---------+----------------+------------+----------------------+---------+

``header_crc`` is the crc32 of the magic and length bytes. It makes a
partial header that borrows bytes from a following frame fail validation,
so an incomplete record in the middle of the log reads as corruption while
a genuinely short final header reads as a torn tail.

Metadata is a compact JSON object: ``{"t":"p","k":key}`` for puts,
``{"t":"d","k":key}`` for deletes, ``{"t":"r","s":start,"e":end}`` for
range tombstones (``null`` marks an unbounded side), ``{"t":"c","s":seq}``
for ordinary commits and ``{"t":"b","s":seq}`` for the base commit that
closes a compacted log. The two carry the sequence identically; a base
marker is additionally required to be the first commit marker in its file.
The raw value bytes follow the first newline, so values need no encoding.

A range tombstone covers every committed key whose raw UTF-8 bytes sort at
or after its start and strictly before its end (half-open). It is resolved
when the log is replayed -- matching keys are popped then -- and, like an
ordinary delete frame, carries no state of its own. Compaction therefore
reclaims it together with every other dead record: the live puts the
compact image contains already exclude each deleted key, so dropping the
tombstone can never make one reappear.
